name: momo_quality
rationale: Momentum carries nearly all of the incumbent's PnL, so improving the *quality* of breakout entries is the highest-leverage structural change available. Today, momentum_donchian fires on any 20-day channel break while the market regime is UP \u2014 including breaks in names that are themselves in downtrends (below their own 200d SMA, negative 6-month return). Those are counter-trend bounces in broken stocks, exactly the population that time-series momentum research (Moskowitz/Ooi/Pedersen; Faber) says has negative expected drift. The incumbent already believes intermediate-term momentum is informative \u2014 it uses 100d return to *rank* candidates \u2014 but when slots are free a negative-momentum name is bought anyway. This experiment turns that ranking belief into an entry gate: only take breakouts where the symbol is above its own 200d SMA and its 126d return is positive. It is a single, theory-grounded filter on one strategy, leaves all exits untouched (open positions can always exit), leaves mean reversion untouched, and should still leave several hundred momentum trades over 10 years. It is distinct from the rejected MR >200sma filter (that one gated dip-buying; this gates breakout-buying, where the trend-persistence logic actually applies) and from the rejected focus-priority tilt (no slot-order manipulation). If it fails, the finding is informative: the round-robin slot mechanism, not entry quality, is what makes momentum work.

name: adaptive_trend_exit
rationale: Momentum carries nearly all of the incumbent's PnL, and last night's attempt to improve momentum *entries* (momo_quality) failed — filters starve the sleeve of its best trades. The untouched lever is the exit. The incumbent exits every breakout on a fixed 10-day channel break regardless of trend context, which is symmetric between a stock chopping sideways after entry and one riding a powerful trend. Trend-following literature is consistent that expectancy comes from the right tail, so exits should be tight when trend quality is poor and loose when it is strong. This experiment changes ONE thing: the momentum sleeve's exit width becomes trend-adaptive — 10-day channel break normally, widened to a 20-day break while ADX(14) > 25 and price is above its own 50d SMA. Losers remain protected by the unchanged 2xATR hard stop enforced by risk.py, so the wider exit only affects trades already working, letting confirmed winners breathe instead of being shaken out on a routine 10-day pullback. Entries, sizing, scores, the MR sleeve, and slot mechanics are all identical, so the arena reads a clean measurement of exit width. Thresholds are textbook (ADX 25, 50d SMA), not fitted, and the rule degrades gracefully to the incumbent when trend data is unavailable.

name: trendfit_rank
rationale: Two straight rejections (momo_quality, adaptive_trend_exit) taught the same lesson: filtering or re-timing momentum entries/exits destroys PnL because the raw Donchian break is already robust. The untouched dimension is *slot allocation* — with 528 symbols, far more breakouts fire each day than there are free slots, so which candidate wins the round-robin slot is decided entirely by score_long, currently raw 100-day return. Ranking by raw return favors gappy, news-spike runs that mean-revert. This experiment changes only the ranking key for momentum: Clenow-style trend-fit score = annualized slope of a 90-day log-price linear regression multiplied by the regression R^2 (well-documented in 'Stocks on the Move'; also consistent with the academic finding that volatility/noise-adjusted momentum outperforms raw momentum). Smooth, persistent trends win slots over erratic spikes. Trade count and the entry/exit rules are untouched, so this is a pure capital-allocation change rather than a filter — no trades are removed, only reprioritized, which is exactly where the previous filter-style experiments lost their winners. Vectorized via cumulative sums (no rolling apply), deterministic, and falls back to the old ret100 score during warmup.

name: dip_trend
rationale: Three straight rejections (momo_quality, adaptive_trend_exit, trendfit_rank) all tried to *filter or re-time the existing momentum leg* and all destroyed PnL — that avenue is closed. Tonight's experiment is purely additive and touches neither momentum's entries/exits nor mean reversion. Findings say momentum carries nearly all PnL while MR is ~breakeven and earns its keep only as a slot occupier; round-robin allocation therefore hands ~half the slots to a breakeven edge. I add a THIRD strategy whose thesis is the trend-following edge captured at a better entry price: in an UP regime, on a stock in confirmed structural uptrend (close>200sma, 50sma>200sma, 100d return>0), buy the first up-close after a fresh 10-day low, then hold with a trend exit (20-day channel break) and the standard 2xATR stop. This is structurally distinct from both incumbents: momentum_donchian buys at 20d *highs* (extension), RSI(2) buys deep 2-day washouts and flips out in <=7 bars at RSI>60, while this leg enters shallow dips inside established trends and lets winners run like momentum does. It differs from the benched fib_pullback (which demanded a deep 38-62% retrace of a 60d swing and hard-exited after 20 days, cutting winners short); here the exit is a trailing channel, which is what makes momentum profitable in this system. If the edge is real it should reclaim slots from breakeven MR candidates without diluting the momentum leg at all; if it dilutes, the arena's full-sample + majority-fold gate rejects it cheaply.

name: mr_momo_rank
rationale: Four consecutive rejections (momo_quality, adaptive_trend_exit, trendfit_rank, dip_trend) all tried to filter or re-time the momentum leg and all destroyed PnL. Clear lesson: leave momentum alone. The untouched lever is the mean-reversion leg, which the findings log says is ~breakeven standalone yet earns its keep purely by *which slots it occupies*. Today MR's slot priority is `buy_below - r2`, i.e. the deepest oversold candidate wins — in a 528-name universe that systematically hands slots to the most violently crashing stocks (falling knives), exactly the population where short-term reversal is weakest. This experiment changes only the ranking key, not the entry set: among the same RSI(2)<10 candidates, the ones with the strongest 6-month return get the slot. No signal is filtered out (the earlier >200sma *filter* failed; a reorder is structurally different because low-quality dips still get taken whenever slots are free), so there is no mechanical PnL removal — only a reallocation of scarce slots toward dips in leaders. Motivation is the well-documented pairing of intermediate-term cross-sectional momentum (Jegadeesh-Titman) with short-horizon reversal (Lehmann/Lo-MacKinlay): buy the pullback, but in names the market is trending up over 6 months. Single-parameter, no calendar logic, no risk changes.

name: slow_trend_leg
rationale:
Five straight rejections (momo_quality, adaptive_trend_exit, trendfit_rank, dip_trend, mr_momo_rank) all modified the existing momentum leg's entries, exits, or ranking — every one destroyed PnL. The lesson is clear: do not touch the 20/10 Donchian leg. But the finding that produced this system's biggest historical gain (11.6% -> 19.7% CAGR) was *slot composition* — adding a second, differently-timed strategy so round-robin allocates capital across independent edges. So tonight's experiment is purely additive: a third leg that runs in parallel and never alters the incumbent two.

The new leg is classic long-horizon time-series momentum (Turtle System-2 style): enter on a 55-day channel breakout in UP regime, only in names above their own 200d SMA with positive 12-month return, exit on a 20-day channel break with a wider 3xATR stop and no time stop. Its economic role is the right tail the fast leg cannot hold: the incumbent's 10d exit and 2xATR stop deliberately cut trends short (which is why adaptive_trend_exit failed when it loosened them — it removed protection from *all* momentum trades). Running a slow, wide-stopped, quality-filtered trend system beside the fast one captures multi-month trends without weakening the fast leg's defense. Sizing stays risk-normalized: a 3xATR stop mechanically means a smaller position for the same risk budget, so the slow leg buys duration, not leverage.

Entries are genuinely differently timed (55d highs with a 200d/12m trend qualifier fire far less often than 20d breaks), rank by 252d return (cross-sectional momentum, the best-evidenced anomaly in the literature), and add a third queue to the round-robin so slot allocation diversifies across horizons instead of alternating between one fast breakout and one 2-day dip. Falsifiable and cheap: if slow trend following adds nothing beyond the fast leg in this universe, the arena rejects it and we stop asking about holding periods.
